query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under high‐temperature sliding in ambient air, the overall wear resistance and local deformation of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings are governed by a synergy between dislocation climb–promoted twin formation beneath the surface and the concurrent formation of a transient, thin protective oxide tribo‐layer. A controlled reduction in Cu content (relative to the optimized baseline) will diminish the efficiency of dislocation climb and lower the density of deformation twins, thereby upsetting this balance and leading to increased plastic damage and higher wear rates—even if a somewhat thicker oxide layer forms—which demonstrates that the intrinsic capacity for twin‐mediated strain accommodation is key.
generation.material_initial_state: Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy thin coating deposited on a conventional metal (e.g., Ni-based) substrate
generation.intervention: Slight compositional modification by reducing Cu content from 13% to approximately 10%, keeping other elements and processing conditions identical
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted at around 600°C in ambient atmospheric conditions (where oxygen is available for tribo-oxidation)
generation.structural_mediator: The density and distribution of nanoscale deformation twins in the subsurface layer and the thickness/adherence of the transient oxide tribo-layer
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, frictional heating facilitates dislocation climb which, in the baseline composition, effectively activates localized twin formation that helps accommodate plastic deformation. At the same time, friction-induced heating in ambient air causes a thin, adherent oxide layer to form that partly shields the surface. Reducing the Cu content is predicted to raise the energy barrier for dislocation climb, thereby lowering twin nucleation. Without robust twin-assisted strain accommodation, the coating is more susceptible to localized plastic deformation and abrasion—even if some oxide forms. Thus, the balance between the intrinsic (twinning) and extrinsic (oxide layer) mechanisms governs wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 coating, the coating with reduced Cu content will exhibit a lower density of deformation twins, evidence of more extensive plastic deformation (e.g., larger or deeper wear scars), and an overall increase in wear rate (and possibly a slight increase in friction coefficient) during high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 HEA coating (with its inherent balance of twin formation and minimal oxide layer formation) under identical high-temperature sliding conditions
generation.boundary: This mechanistic interplay is expected to dominate at high temperatures around 600°C in an oxygen‐rich (ambient) atmosphere. At room temperature or under inert atmosphere conditions where tribo-oxidation is suppressed, the balance and the associated wear mechanisms may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The proposal extends MD and mechanical simulation findings on twin formation in FeNiCrCoCu HEAs (e.g., from PMC10058552::web::024::4_conclusions) and contrasts them with high-temperature wear observations that emphasize protective oxide or glaze layer formation (e.g., PMC10241162::web::014::remarkable_wear_resistance_and_wear_mech). Although each mechanism is supported by prior studies, combining them as a synergistic mechanism driven by a controlled compositional change (via Cu reduction) is new and has not been directly tested. Uncertainty remains regarding the quantitative relationship between Cu content, twin nucleation efficiency, and oxide layer properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on identical conventional metal substrates: one with the baseline composition (Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13) and one with reduced Cu (Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu10). Subject both sets to high-temperature (≈600°C) reciprocating sliding wear tests in ambient air at identical normal loads and sliding speeds. Following testing, perform detailed post-mortem analysis using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify the subsurface density of deformation twins and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess the thickness and continuity of any oxide layer.
measurements: Wear scar depth and volume (quantitative wear rate)
Density and spatial distribution of deformation twins (via TEM)
Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via EDS mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified (reduced Cu) coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in twin density accompanied by an increase in wear rate and evidence of enhanced plastic deformation relative to the baseline coating—or if the oxide layer properties appear to fully compensate for the reduction in twins such that wear resistance is maintained—then the hypothesis that twin-mediated strain accommodation is a critical contributor to the overall wear resistance under these conditions is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu HEAs with unequal atomic ratio are studied by combining ML and MD. Among the three ML algorithms (MLR, BPNN, RF) adopted, the MLR model performed well in predicting tensile strength of FeNiCrCoCu HEAs. This is attributed to strong linear correlation between tensile strength of the HEAs and the content of principal elements. Mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu HEAs with unequal atomic ratio were predicted using the optimal MLR model, and tensile strength of Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 HEAs (HEAs with optimum mechanical properties) reached 28.25 GPa. ML results were verified using MD, and it was found that error between predicted tensile strength and the simulated was within 0.5%. The FeNiCrCoCu HEAs were simulated for tension-compression at different temperatures and composition ratios. We found that the influence of temperature on the tensile and compressive mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu HEAs is greater than the influence of the content of the primary element. cited_evidence.text: No micro-pits or debris are observed from the Ni3X surface away from the worn track (Fig. S9), confirming that they are indeed generated during sliding. For NiX, its worn track dimensions also increase at 400 °C compared to those at RT, but the worn surface remains relatively smooth and is free of debris and micro-pits (Fig. S7b). This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa).
